migrationNotes: Spine: a bank statement shows the balance so far on each line, and the lesson follows that one statement from a running total, to rows that tie in the ordering, to a look at the row before and the row after, and the blanks those can give.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-running-totals-and-neighbours-8 (a running sum over 4, 6 and 8). It repeats the first screen's idea and the check on the bank statement tests it.

lesson.title: Read the rows before and after

lead.text: Think about the statement again. Each balance is a sum, but a different set of rows is added at every line: one deposit at line one, two at line two, three at line three. The window needs a way to say which rows to add for the row it is on.

That is the frame, the stretch of the window that the calculation uses for the current row. Writing ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW sets the frame to every row from the start of the window down to the current one. SUM over that frame gives a running total, a sum that grows by one row at each step. The ORDER BY inside OVER matters here, because it decides which row is first and so which rows count as coming before.

afterFigure.text: The figure follows a money jar with four deposits: 20, 5, 15 and 10. The running total, 20, 25, 40 and 50, is the sum of the frame at each line. As with any SUM, an unknown amount adds nothing and does not stop the total growing on later lines. The jar also records the day of each deposit, and two questions from now that column starts to matter.

queries.label: The whole total on every row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM jar ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The total so far
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each line adds one more row to the frame. Work out the third line of the statement.
The shop's orders in id order. The frame runs from the first order to the current one, and the last amount is unknown, so it adds nothing.

reveal.text: You added the rows up to and including the current one. The grand total would use every row at once.

queries.label: Known grand total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER () AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Running known total
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Rows that tie in the order

lead.text: One detail of the frame needs care when two rows tie in the ordering. Look at the money jar: two deposits were made on day 2. If the window is ordered by day alone, nothing says which of the two comes first.

ROWS counts physical rows. It takes them one at a time, so the first of the two day-2 deposits gets its own running total and the second adds to it. RANGE works by value instead. Rows that tie on the ordering value are called peers, and RANGE treats them as a single step, so every peer joins the frame together. Both day-2 deposits show the same running total, which includes the pair in full.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the first query gives 20, 25, 40 and 50, and the second gives 20, 40, 40 and 50. They agree everywhere except across the tied pair. When a window has an ORDER BY and no frame is written, SQL uses the RANGE version, so a running total over a column with repeats can jump by two rows at once. Writing the ROWS frame yourself removes the surprise.

queries.label: Counting rows
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: Counting by day
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM jar ORDER BY day, id;

lead.text: Decide which rows the frame holds for each of the two September 2 orders.

queries.label: ROWS frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

queries.label: RANGE frame
queries.sql: SELECT id, day, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS total FROM orders ORDER BY day, id;

lead.text: A frame adds rows up. Sometimes a report needs a single neighbour instead, such as the previous deposit, to see how the new one compares. LAG(amount) returns the amount from the row before the current one in the window's order.

The first row has nothing before it, so LAG gives NULL there. The order inside OVER decides what before means, so the same table read in the opposite order hands back different neighbours. Read the jar's deposits from newest to oldest and the row before a deposit is the one made after it.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the jar read both ways. In day order the second deposit sees 20 behind it. Read backwards, the first deposit sees 5, because 5 sits one row earlier in that reversed order. Subtract LAG's value from the current amount and you have the change since the previous line.

queries.label: Reading forwards
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM jar ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Reading backwards
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM jar ORDER BY id DESC;

lead.text: The shop's orders, read in increasing id order. LAG looks one row back.

reveal.text: You read one row back in the stated order. Reversing the order would change which row counts as previous.

queries.label: Previous in increasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ASC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id ASC;

queries.label: Previous in decreasing id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id DESC) AS previous FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC;

steps.headline: Looking ahead, and what a blank means

lead.text: LEAD is the mirror of LAG. It returns the value from the next row in the window's order, and the last row has nothing after it, so LEAD gives NULL there. Between them, LAG and LEAD let a row see both of its neighbours without a join.

A NULL from either function has two possible causes. There may be no neighbour in that direction, as at the ends. Or the neighbour is there and its own value is unknown. Take a water meter read on three days: 12 litres on day 1, no reading on day 2 and 9 litres on day 3. LEAD of the litres gives NULL on day 1 and on day 3, for different reasons. Day 2's reading is missing, and nothing follows day 3.

afterFigure.text: To tell the two causes apart, read a column that is always filled in. LEAD of the day number is NULL only where no next row exists, so the figure shows it beside LEAD of the litres. A NULL in the first and a number in the second means the neighbour is there and its value is missing.

queries.label: The next reading
queries.sql: SELECT id, litres, LEAD(litres) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_litres FROM meter ORDER BY id;

queries.label: The next day
queries.sql: SELECT id, litres, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM meter ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Back in the shop's orders, in increasing id order. LEAD looks one row ahead.

queries.label: Next amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Next id
queries.sql: SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lesson.orientation: Specify running frames and use LAG or LEAD with an explicit ordering.
lesson.reviewLabel: Read the rows before and after
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A bank statement lists three deposits in the order they were made: 30 pounds, then 10, then 50. Beside each deposit the bank prints the balance, the amount in the account as of that line.

The balance on the first line is 30, since nothing came before it. On the second line it covers the first deposit and the second. Each line adds one more deposit to what came before, so the figure beside a line depends on the lines above it, and reading the statement from the bottom up would give different numbers.

The totals in the last lesson covered a whole group at once. A statement needs a total that grows down the page, and it invites a second kind of comparison too, between a line and its neighbours, such as how much more a deposit was than the one before. This final lesson adds both to the window.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add up the rows so far, and look at the rows just before and after.

recap.keyIdea: A frame decides which rows a window value adds, and LAG and LEAD read the neighbours in the stated order. A NULL there can mean no neighbour or no value.

blocks.text: You reached a balance of 90, then a running total of 180 at order 103. LAG gave 80 at order 104 and LEAD gave 40 at order 103.

recap.nextHook: You have now taken a table from rows to a finished report. Each lesson added one more thing a query can do, and the reports you write next will use them together.

questions.prompt: Taking the shop's orders in increasing id order, what is the running total of the known amounts at order 103?
hints: Include rows through 103, not later rows.
Add the first three known amounts.
Evaluate 80 + 20 + 80; later ids are outside this frame.
questions.onCorrect: 180. The frame runs from the first row to order 103, so it adds three amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops at order 102. The frame includes order 103 itself.
That is the grand total. A running total stops at the current row.

questions.prompt: The shop's orders are summed with a RANGE frame ordered by day, and orders 102 and 103 were both placed on 2 September. Why do both rows show the same total?
hints: Rows with equal window ordering values are peers.

acceptedIdeas: The frame includes both rows with the same day
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The RANGE frame includes peers with the same ordering value. Both September 2 rows include the whole day and share its cumulative total of 180.

choices.label: The frame includes both rows with the same day
SUM always returns the grand total

questions.onCorrect: The frame includes both rows with the same day. Rows tied in the order are peers under RANGE.

misconceptions.feedback: Here SUM covers only the frame, which grows row by row.
The ids are untouched. The day decides which rows count together.

questions.prompt: With increasing ids, what does LAG(amount) return at order 104?
hints: LAG reads the previous row in the window order.
Use order 103's amount, not order 104's amount.
Read the amount on order 103; it precedes 104 in the specified order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The preceding row is order 103, whose amount is 80.

questions.onCorrect: 80. LAG reads the amount on the previous row, order 103.

misconceptions.feedback: That is two rows back. LAG reads the previous row.
That is order 104's own amount. LAG reads the row before it.

questions.prompt: With increasing ids, what does LEAD(amount) return at order 103?
hints: LEAD reads the next row in the window order.
Use order 104's amount.
Read the amount on order 104; it follows 103 in the specified order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The next row is order 104, whose amount is 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. LEAD reads the amount on the next row, order 104.

misconceptions.feedback: That is order 103's own amount. LEAD reads the next row.
That is two rows ahead. LEAD reads only the next row.

questions.prompt: Ordered amounts are 10, NULL and 30. What is the running SUM at the third row?
hints: SUM ignores NULL values.
Add known amounts from the first row through the third.
Add the known values 10 and 30; the NULL cell contributes no known value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known contributing amounts are 10 and 30. Their running sum is 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. The NULL adds nothing, so the sum is the known 10 and 30.

misconceptions.feedback: SUM keeps adding after a NULL. The third row is still in the frame.

questions.prompt: A LEAD(amount) value is NULL. What can you conclude from that value alone?
hints: Compare LEAD(id) if you need to distinguish no next row from a missing next amount.

acceptedIdeas: The next amount may be missing, or there may be no next row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With its default, LEAD returns NULL when no next row exists. A next row whose amount is NULL produces the same value, so NULL alone cannot distinguish the cases.

choices.label: There is definitely no next row
The next amount may be missing, or there may be no next row

questions.onCorrect: The next amount may be missing, or there may be no next row. One NULL has two possible causes.

misconceptions.feedback: The next amount may be unknown too. NULL alone cannot tell you which.
Zero is a known amount. A NULL is not a zero.

questions.prompt: A statement lists deposits of 30, 10 and 50 pounds in order. Each line shows the balance so far. What balance does the statement show after the third deposit?
hints: What does a balance include?
It adds every deposit so far.
Add the first three deposits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Deposits of 30, 10 and 50 add up to a balance of 90 after the third.

questions.onCorrect: 90. A balance adds everything so far, up to the current line. A running total does the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the third deposit alone. The balance adds everything so far.

questions.prompt: A running SUM over the amounts 4, 6 and 8, in that order, is shown beside each row. What does it show at the second row?
hints: Which rows does the frame include at the second row?
It runs from the first row to the current row.
Add the first two amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the second row the frame holds 4 and 6, which add up to 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The frame runs from the first row to the current one, so each row adds one more amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second amount alone. A running total adds the rows up to this one.

questions.prompt: Ordered amounts are 7, 9 and 12. What does LAG(amount) show at the third row?
hints: Which direction does LAG read?
LAG reads the previous row.
Which amount sits just before the third row?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row before the third holds 9, so LAG(amount) shows 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. LAG reads the row before the current one in the window order.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the third row's own amount. LAG reads the row before it.
That is two rows back. LAG reads only the previous row.
